lessons.title: A structured approach to fault finding
lessons.html:
Why guessing costs money

Replacing parts until a fault disappears is expensive for the customer, wastes workshop time and often leaves the real cause unfixed. A farmer waiting for a tractor in planting season loses money every day. A structured approach finds faults faster and builds customer trust.

The seven-step method

  1. Gather information: interview the operator. When does the fault happen? Hot or cold? Under load? Since when? Any recent work or fuel delivery?
  2. Verify the fault: see, hear or measure it yourself, ideally under the same conditions.
  3. Check the basics: fluid levels, filters, battery, visible damage, leaks, loose connections, service history.
  4. Gather data: fault codes, live data, pressure readings, compression or leak-down tests, oil analysis.
  5. Analyse: list possible causes, starting with the most likely and easiest to check. Use the service manual's troubleshooting charts and system diagrams.
  6. Test and repair: prove the cause before replacing parts. Repair to manufacturer specifications.
  7. Verify and record: confirm the fault is gone under working conditions and record the cause, fix and parts on the job card.

Root cause thinking

Ask why repeatedly. A turbo failed. Why? Lack of oil. Why? The oil feed line was blocked by sludge. Why? Oil changes were overdue. The root cause is maintenance practice; replacing only the turbo would lead to another failure. Report root causes to the customer with advice.

Tools of the trade

  • Multimeter and oscilloscope for electrical signals.
  • Diagnostic software for codes and live data.
  • Pressure gauges for hydraulics, fuel and boost.
  • Compression and cylinder leak-down testers.
  • Infrared thermometer for temperature differences between cylinders or components.
  • Oil analysis reports showing wear metals, fuel dilution, coolant or dust.

lessons.title: Optimising engine performance and efficiency
lessons.html:
What engine optimisation means

Optimisation is getting the rated power, best fuel economy and longest life from an engine within the manufacturer's specifications. Diesel is one of a farm's largest costs, so a tractor using more fuel than it should costs the farmer a lot over a season.

Common causes of low power or high fuel use

AreaTypical causes
AirBlocked air filter, intake leaks, faulty turbo, restricted intercooler
FuelBlocked filters, water in fuel, worn injectors, low rail pressure, air leaks
ExhaustRestricted exhaust or blocked DPF, faulty EGR
Engine conditionLow compression, worn rings, incorrect valve clearances
CoolingBlocked radiator or faulty thermostat causing derate
ElectronicsSensor faults causing derate, outdated software
OperationWrong gear and engine speed, poor ballast, wheel slip, wrong tyre pressure

Testing performance

A PTO dynamometer measures actual power at the PTO and lets you compare it with the rating. Fuel consumption can be measured on the dyno or from engine data. Compare results before and after repairs. Measure boost, rail pressure and exhaust temperature with the diagnostic tool during the test.

Working with operators

Many efficiency gains come from how the tractor is used. Advise operators to use gear-up throttle-down for light work, avoid long idling, set tyre pressures and ballast for the job and keep wheel slip within the range the manufacturer recommends. Explain that a clean air filter and radiator matter in dusty and chaff-heavy conditions.

Limits

Never adjust fuel delivery or software beyond the manufacturer's specifications to gain power. Over-fuelling raises exhaust temperatures, damages pistons and turbos, voids warranty and can breach emissions requirements. Use only authorised software updates.

Key points

  • Follow a structured fault-finding method instead of replacing parts by guesswork.
  • Prove the cause before replacing parts, then verify and record the fix.
  • Ask why repeatedly to find the root cause.
  • Check air, fuel, exhaust, engine condition, cooling, electronics and operation for power loss.
  • Stay within manufacturer specifications when optimising.
